title: QSSR Enhancements Unveiled for Six PS5 Titles, Now Live in Marvel’s Spider‑Man 2 – Digital Foundry
body:
Sony’s latest image‑upscaling solution, dubbed QSSR (Quick Super Sampling Rendering), is now live in six PlayStation 5 titles, with Marvel’s Spider‑Man 2 leading the charge. The technology, which originated from the same “Project Amethyst” partnership between Sony and AMD that birthed the higher‑resolution PSSR mode for the PS5 Pro, promises sharper visuals and smoother performance on the standard PS5 hardware without the need for a console upgrade. A recent PlayStation blog post explains why developers are embracing AI‑driven upscaling, and early impressions suggest the move could set a new baseline for next‑gen console graphics.

QSSR works by rendering games at a lower internal resolution and then using a machine‑learning algorithm to reconstruct a higher‑resolution image that retains fine details and reduces jagged edges. Unlike traditional spatial upscaling, which simply stretches pixels, QSSR leverages a neural network trained on a massive library of Sony‑optimized textures and lighting data. The result is an image that looks close to native 4K while demanding far less GPU horsepower. For developers, the benefit is twofold: they can maintain or even raise frame‑rate targets while delivering a visual fidelity that rivals the PS5 Pro’s PSSR mode, all without rewriting large portions of their rendering pipelines.

Insomniac Games was the first to integrate QSSR into a live title, rolling it out as an optional “Performance‑Plus” mode in Marvel’s Spider‑Man 2. Players who enable the setting report crisper character models, more detailed cityscapes, and a noticeable reduction in texture pop‑in, especially during fast‑paced combat sequences. The mode also preserves the game’s 60 fps target, a critical factor for a title that relies heavily on fluid movement and precise timing. Following Insomniac’s lead, five other developers have announced updates for their PS5 releases, including titles from the studios behind “Horizon Forbidden West,” “Resident Evil Village,” and “Gran Turismo 7.” Each update arrives as a downloadable patch, meaning owners of the base console can instantly benefit from the enhancement without purchasing new hardware.

The rollout arrives at a pivotal moment for Sony, which is still promoting the PS5 Pro as the premium upgrade for enthusiasts seeking higher resolutions and ray‑tracing fidelity. By bringing a form of AI‑upscaling to the standard PS5, Sony effectively narrows the visual gap between the two systems, extending the lifespan of its larger install base. Analysts see this as a strategic move to keep the PS5 ecosystem vibrant while the company prepares for the next generation of consoles. Moreover, the PlayStation blog highlights that QSSR’s low overhead makes it attractive for indie developers and mid‑tier studios that lack the resources to implement more complex rendering techniques.

Industry observers note that AI‑driven upscaling is becoming a mainstream tool across platforms, with competitors such as Nvidia’s DLSS and AMD’s FSR already entrenched in PC gaming. Sony’s entry into the space underscores a broader shift toward software‑centric performance gains rather than relying solely on raw hardware power. The company’s collaboration with AMD ensures that the underlying tensor cores in the PS5’s GPU can be efficiently harnessed, and the partnership may pave the way for future iterations that further refine image quality or reduce latency.

Looking ahead, the success of QSSR could influence how upcoming titles are built from the ground up, with developers designing assets and shaders that are optimized for AI‑upscaled pipelines. If player reception remains positive, Sony may expand the technology beyond visual fidelity, potentially applying similar neural‑network approaches to audio processing or physics simulation. For now, the immediate impact is clear: PS5 owners can experience a noticeable visual boost in some of the platform’s flagship games, reinforcing Sony’s commitment to delivering next‑gen experiences without forcing a hardware upgrade. As more patches roll out and new games launch with QSSR baked in, the line between console generations may blur, ushering in an era where intelligent software enhancements keep the PlayStation ecosystem fresh and competitive.
